title: First aid awareness and reporting accidents
siteNotes: Who the first aiders (or the appointed person) are on each shift, and how to reach them
Where the first aid boxes are, and who restocks them
Where the accident book is kept and who may see it
The venue's address and how to describe the entrance for an ambulance
Who the manager on duty is for reporting purposes and who makes RIDDOR reports
Where defibrillator is, if the venue has one
legalNotes: Employers must provide adequate and appropriate equipment, facilities and people for first aid, based on a needs assessment: Health and Safety (First-Aid) Regulations 1981. https://www.hse.gov.uk/firstaid/ (HSE first aid FAQ checked).
An appointed person looks after equipment and calls the emergency services but is not a first aider and should not give first aid they are not trained for: HSE first aid FAQ (checked).
First aiders generally do not give tablets or medicines; the specific exceptions are not taught here. HSE first aid FAQ (checked).

Calling 999 for serious cases and not moving a seriously injured person unless in danger: standard NHS and first aid training advice (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/first-aid/). Not checked on a specific page in this session. No clinical first aid is taught.

RIDDOR 2013: the 'responsible person' (usually the employer or person in control of premises) reports. Reportable cases include deaths, specified (serious) injuries, injuries causing over seven days off work, members of the public taken straight to hospital from the premises, and dangerous occurrences. https://www.hse.gov.uk/riddor/ . The HSE pages could not be loaded in detail here, so this is from established knowledge and must be confirmed. Reporting deadlines are deliberately not stated in the slides.

The accident book: employers with ten or more employees must keep one; other employers are advised to. Under the Social Security (Claims and Payments) Regulations 1979. Not confirmed in this session, and the slides do not state the ten-employee rule; they simply teach to record every accident in the accident book.
Accident book entries hold personal data and must be kept confidential: HSE accident book guidance (INDG174 could not be loaded here); flagged as not verified.
Near misses are not legally reportable in most cases but are good practice to record and learn from: HSE advice. Not checked on a specific page.
First aiders need an approved First Aid at Work or Emergency First Aid at Work course (see index.json).

Review Oct 2026: 'approved' first aid course changed to 'recognised ... from a competent training provider'. HSE stopped approving first aid training providers in 2013; the employer must choose a competent provider. The index entry still says 'approved'.

Review Oct 2026: HSE FAQ confirms an appointed person does not need first aid training and must not give first aid they are not trained for (slide edited to say 'not required to be a first aider'). The First-Aid Regulations do not oblige employers to provide first aid for the public, but HSE strongly recommends including them, which is why the venue treats guests the same.

Review Oct 2026: slide 4 was an absolute 'do not give medicine or move the person'. That would be wrong for an anaphylaxis or asthma emergency (helping with the person's own adrenaline pen or inhaler) and when a 999 call handler instructs the caller (recovery position, CPR). Softened to allow those. The allergens session already teaches the auto-injector.

Review Oct 2026: RIDDOR slide checked against HSE: over-7-day incapacitation (not counting the day of the accident), specified injuries, deaths, dangerous occurrences, and non-workers taken directly from the scene to hospital for treatment are reportable by the responsible person. The slide's 'guests taken straight to hospital' matches, but only where the accident arose from the work activity; the manager decides. Deadlines remain unstated. Accident book: HSE INDG453 confirms recording of accidents is required; the 10-or-more-employees rule for the formal accident book (Social Security (Claims and Payments) Regulations 1979, reg. 25) could not be re-read this session. Recording every accident including guests is venue policy/good practice and is taught as such.

cards.title: First aid awareness and reporting accidents
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- find help quickly in an emergency
- know what to do, and what not to do, until help arrives
- record every accident and near miss

cards.title: Everyone has a part to play
cards.body:
You do not need to be a first aider to help. Knowing who they are, how to call for help and how to record what happened is part of every role. Guests, colleagues and contractors can all be affected.

> This session is awareness only. It does not make you a first aider.

items.title: Find help
items.text: Know who the first aiders are.

items.title: Record
items.text: Every accident and near miss is written down.

cards.title: First aiders and the first aid box
cards.body:
A first aider has completed a recognised first aid course (First Aid at Work or Emergency First Aid at Work) from a competent training provider. Some workplaces have an appointed person instead, who looks after the first aid box and calls the emergency services but should not give first aid they are not trained for.

> Your manager will show you who the first aiders are, where the first aid boxes are, and how to reach them on your shift.

right.title: Appointed person
items: Not required to be a first aider

cards.title: Serious? Call 999 first
cards.body:
If someone is seriously hurt or ill, call 999 straight away, or ask someone else to while you stay with the person. Then call a first aider. Stay calm and give clear details.

> Your manager will show you how to describe the venue's entrance for an ambulance.

items.title: Call 999
items.text: Or send someone to do it.

items.title: Meet the crew
items.text: Send someone to the entrance to guide them in.

cards.title: Do not make it worse
cards.body: Do not move someone who is seriously injured unless they are in danger, for example from fire, or the 999 call handler or a first aider tells you to. Do not give food or drink, and do not give medicine unless a first aider or the 999 call handler tells you to. The exception is helping someone use their own emergency medication, such as an inhaler or adrenaline pen. Do not leave them alone. Leave treatment to a first aider or the ambulance crew.

left.title: Do
items: Keep the area safe and clear

right.title: Do not
items: Move them unless in danger or told to

cards.title: The accident book
cards.body:
Every accident or injury to a colleague, guest or contractor, however small, is written in the accident book. Say what happened, when, where, who was hurt and what was done. Entries are private; do not share them.

> Your manager will show you where the accident book is kept.

cards.title: A near miss is a free warning
cards.body: A near miss is when something nearly hurt someone, such as a tray dropped beside a guest, or a wet floor someone almost slipped on. Nobody was hurt, but the next person may not be so lucky. Tell your manager so it can be put right.

items.title: Injury
items.text: Someone is hurt. Record and act.

items.title: Near miss
items.text: Nobody hurt, but it nearly happened.

cards.title: RIDDOR: your manager reports it
cards.body: Some accidents must be reported to the HSE by the employer or person in charge. This includes deaths, serious injuries, people off work for more than seven days, guests taken straight to hospital, and certain dangerous events. You do not make the report. You do tell your manager at once.

items.title: Serious injury
items.text: Tell your manager, who decides on a report.

items.title: Time off work
items.text: Tell your manager if you are off after an accident.

items.title: Dangerous event
items.text: For example a fire, gas leak or collapse.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Know who the first aiders are
- Serious: call 999 first, and stay with the person
- Do not move a seriously injured person unless in danger
- Record every accident and near miss in the accident book
- Tell your manager at once about serious injuries: they handle RIDDOR

cards.q: A guest collapses in the bar and is not responding. What should you do first?
options: Move them to a quieter room
Wait a few minutes to see if they come round
Give them a drink of water
Ring 999 or send someone to, and call a first aider
cards.why: In a serious case, call 999 straight away and get a first aider. Do not move them or give anything to drink.

cards.q: You should move a seriously injured person to a more comfortable place as soon as you can.
cards.why: Only move them if they are in danger, such as from fire. Otherwise leave that to a first aider or the ambulance crew.

cards.q: A colleague drops a tray and cuts their hand slightly, then says 'don't make a fuss'. What happens?
options: Nothing, it is minor
Only a manager can write it down privately
It is recorded in the accident book
It is recorded if they need stitches
cards.why: Every accident, however small, is recorded. It protects the person if it becomes a problem later.

cards.q: Which TWO are true about reporting accidents?
options: Staff make the RIDDOR report themselves
Near misses should be reported to your manager
Only accidents to guests need recording
The manager handles RIDDOR reports for serious cases
You should discuss accident book entries with other guests
cards.why: You tell your manager about near misses and serious cases. The employer or person in charge makes any RIDDOR report.

cards.q: What is the difference between a first aider and an appointed person?
options: A first aider is trained to treat; an appointed person manages the kit and calls for help
There is no difference, as both are trained to give the same treatment on shift
An appointed person is more senior and can overrule a first aider on treatment
A first aider only has to be on site when the kitchen is open and cooking
cards.why: A first aider has completed an approved course. An appointed person takes charge when needed and calls emergency services, but should not give first aid they are not trained for.

cards.q: A first aid box on its own means the business does not need to tell staff who their first aiders are.
cards.why: Staff need to know the arrangements, including who the first aiders are and where help and equipment are.

cards.q: A guest has a nosebleed and is unsteady on their feet. After calling a first aider, what should you do?
options: Stay with them and keep them calm
Take them to their room alone
Give them a glass of brandy
Ask them to wait outside
cards.why: Do not leave an injured or unwell person alone, and do not give drinks or medicine.

cards.q: A chef says they have a sore wrist from lifting, but nothing happened on the spot. What should happen?
options: Nothing yet, they might be fine
Wait a week then report it
Ask the guest to sign it
They should record it in the accident book
cards.why: Accidents and injuries are recorded, so there is a record if it becomes a problem later.

cards.q: If a guest is taken straight from the premises to hospital after an accident, you should tell your manager immediately.
cards.why: This may be reportable under RIDDOR by the responsible person, so the manager needs to know at once.

cards.q: A glass is knocked off a shelf and lands next to a guest but misses them. What do you do?
options: Nothing, nobody was hurt
Only write it down if the guest complains
Tell your manager so it is recorded and fixed
Tell the guest not to worry
cards.why: Near misses are free warnings: report them so the cause is put right.
